00 Executive summary

The page a hiring manager reads first.

The 30-second version

Home Depot staff filed incidents through a web app that minted a ServiceNow ticket, then manually re-created the incident in Slack and emailed responders, who finally dialed into a conference bridge. The act of reporting had become slower than the act of resolving. I led design on an incident management system — an On-Call assistant living natively in Teams that turns reporting, notifying, and assembling the war-room into one continuous flow, while ServiceNow quietly stays the system of record.

Domain
IT / Ops incident response
Surface
Teams bot + adaptive cards
Scope
MVP · full lifecycle
Role
Lead PD · research→spec
What I owned
  • Reframed the brief — from "build a faster form" to "compress the first five minutes."
  • Designed the atomic unit — one adaptive card that is the alert, the status, and the door to the call.
  • Three invocation paths — bot command, message action, proactive card — one for every way work surfaces.
  • A governed lifecycle — workstreams, four states, and a locked close that stops noise on resolved incidents.
01 Context · the world before

The team already lived in Teams. The incident process didn't.

Home Depot's on-call responders coordinate everything else — code, decisions, releases — inside Microsoft Teams. But the moment something broke, the process flung them outward: a web form, a ServiceNow ticket, a Slack message typed by hand, an email blast, a Webex bridge. Five surfaces, none talking to each other, all between the responder and the fix.

Role 01 · Incident reporter

The one who notices

First to see the symptom. Wants to raise the alarm in seconds and get back to triage — not learn a ticketing schema. Needs status visibility after filing.

Role 02 · Incident manager

The one who coordinates

Owns the response. Needs the full picture, the ability to assign workstreams and drive status, and one place to close and lock the record — without chasing five threads.

Per the brief, the MVP served exactly two roles. Resisting persona-inflation kept the flows honest.

02 Problem

The slowest part of incident response is the part before anyone responds.

Resolution is hard work that needs experts. Starting resolution should be trivial — yet it had become a relay across tools, where every handoff added delay and a chance to drop something. We named this the fragmentation tax: the minutes paid to coordination before a single diagnostic step is taken.

03 Research

Five findings. One of them rewrote the brief.

The brief arrived as "build a faster intake form." Before drawing a single field, I ran a process audit and grounded the work in six pointed questions sent to Home Depot — asking for the actual artifacts of their current process, so every design decision answered to reality.

The six questions that grounded the work

I asked Home Depot for the evidence, not opinions — the real screenshots and lists behind their current process. Every answer became a constraint the design had to honor.

Q1

The live ServiceNow flow

Every field on the current ticket — so nothing essential is lost in translation.

Q2

Workstreams

What fields, and why — the unit of parallel response work.

Q3

Conference bridges

How responders connect today via Webex — the join we must preserve.

Q4

The email confirmation

What's sent on ticket creation — the notification to replace.

Q5

Managers & bridges

Who manages incidents, and the full list of bridge lines.

Q6

How many roles?

Reporter and manager — the two we designed distinct paths for.

04 Process

A five-phase sprint, deliberately front-loaded on understanding.

Two-thirds of the timeline went to framing and structure before any high-fidelity pixels — because in incident response, a wrong information model costs more than a wrong colour. Each phase ended in an artifact a stakeholder could react to.

02

05 Solution

The whole incident — ticket, team, and call — inside one Teams conversation.

This is the incident management system — an On-Call assistant. It doesn't replace ServiceNow; it makes it invisible. A reporter expresses intent in plain steps; the system files the ticket, posts a live card, notifies the right people, and hands everyone the same door into the Webex war-room.

Four principles that settled every argument
01

Meet people where they already are

If the team lives in Teams, the incident lives in Teams. Zero new destinations.

02

Make the system of record invisible

ServiceNow still owns the ticket — but nobody re-keys data or opens a second tab to create it.

03

Notify with an action, not an FYI

Every alert carries the buttons to act — view, update, change status, join — so reading and responding are one motion.

04

Design for the worst five minutes

High pressure, low patience. Smart defaults, few taps, the happy path is the fast path.

Three ways in · one destination

Whichever way a problem surfaces, it becomes the same incident card

The brief named three scenarios — bot automation, proactive notifications, message actions. Each serves a different moment of noticing.

Component anatomy

One card does the work of an email, a status page, and a meeting invite

  • 1

    Priority + state, top-right

    "High priority · New" answers is this urgent, is this live? before you read a word. Recognition over recall.

  • 2

    ID# — the ServiceNow spine, surfaced

    The real ticket number is shown but never re-keyed. The system of record stays authoritative and invisible.

  • 3

    Conference bridge, one tap

    The Webex line rides on the card — no hunting for a dial-in. The war-room is a click, not a search.

  • 4

    Action buttons, not an FYI

    View workstream · Change status · inline activity update. Reading and responding are the same motion.

★ Leadership & influence

What I owned beyond the pixels.

Reframed the ask

Pushed back on "faster form" with a process audit, and got the client to fund the real problem — coordination, not data entry. The lollipop chart was the artifact that won the room.

Aligned two roles + platform

Reporter, manager, and the platform team each wanted a different "first screen." The service blueprint gave us one shared map to negotiate scope against.

Set the system, not the screen

Defined the incident object and its four states once, so every surface — card, dashboard, notification — inherited the same truth. That's what made the MVP buildable on the timeline.

09 Reflection

What I'd carry forward.

The strongest design move on this project wasn't a screen — it was refusing to build the screen we were asked for until we'd proven it was the wrong one.— the lesson I keep
  • Instrument it next time. The MVP shipped without telemetry on time-to-respond. I'd build the measurement into v1 so the hypothesis becomes a result.
  • The locked close earned its keep. Stakeholders doubted a hard lock; it became the most-praised detail — governance that feels like care, not control.
  • One object, many doors. Collapsing every entry onto a single incident object is the pattern I now reach for in any multi-surface system.

From

  • Five fragmented tools
  • Reporting slower than resolving
  • Data re-keyed by hand
  • “Who's even responding?”

To

We redesigned how the first five minutes get spent.
